title: I Am the Storm
mood: At the edge of the widening crack, Obsidia shows Vexana a broken suit and the storm she rides.

hero.alt: Obsidia's pale hair streams sideways in a storm wind, a fork of lightning splitting the dark behind her.

segs.t: “The gate. Now.”
The mark had spoken in the hollow. Now Vexana stood at the edge of the crack, so close that the city’s glow fell through it onto her robe.
From the hollow the crack looked small. Up close, its four points ran off into the dark farther than she could follow.
Through it lay the bay at night, and the shore lights of Terrinia.
A wind came through from the other side. It smelled of rain on stone.
Off to one side lay the body, the Mother Matrix, vast and still. Nothing on it moved. But the torn edges of the crack trembled, and each time they settled, more sky showed.
At the middle of the star the shore lights bent aside, the way water parts around a stone. In the bend there was no light at all.

media.alt: A four-pointed tear of violet light hangs open across a dark, clouded sky, its points running off out of sight and its middle black.

segs.t: Each time she saw the crack, there was less time left to search.

Twice since the hanging streets she had gone to the rows. Both times she kept to their edge, as if only passing. Every Ender in them had eyes, and what they saw ran up the line. She had seen none of them being made, and no Core.
“Come up.”
The voice came from above. Beside the body hung the Storm Citadel. Its prow, the foremost of its black blocks, reached out of the storm toward the gate, high over her head.
From up there she could still see the crack. She would still be where she was sent.
The body is one enemy,
she thought.
That ship is the other.
She leaned toward it, and the dark lifted her.
No Ender stood on the prow. In its middle lay a slab of black plate, and on the slab lay an Aspirant suit.
It was scorched black. One arm was gone. Its shoulder plate was stamped S·L·K.
She knew it. Out in the dead ground she had stood over a ditch and watched two feeders drag it out by the legs. The hand that was left was still a fist.
Obsidia floated beside the slab, one palm laid over the suit’s chest. Under the palm sat its core, dark and cracked.
A low hum came up through the prow. Vexana felt it in her teeth.
Under Obsidia’s hand it glowed violet, rising and falling. It sank into the core, where a pilot’s belief had once lit it, and went no further.
The plates stayed dark and silent. Only the core answered, with a faint tick, like metal cooling.
Obsidia did not look up. “Your people’s suits are made of my kind,” she said. “Did you know?”
“Everyone knows.”
“You wake our dead with what you believe. Not with fire. Not with current. Only that.”
“We use what you leave,” said Vexana.
“So do I. This is the first of your machines I have held.”
I let them take it,
Vexana thought.
Now it lies here.
“What are you doing to it?”
Obsidia did not answer. The hum fell. The core ticked.
Vexana found that her own hand had closed. She opened it.
“Did you know its pilot?” said Obsidia, still without looking up.
“No.”
“Your hand did.”
“How does it move?” said Vexana. “This ship.”
Obsidia lifted one finger from the suit.
Lightning came out of the storm and ran down across the prow. It cracked along the plate a step from Vexana’s boots and went out.
“I am the storm,” said Obsidia.
Vexana did not step back.
Hers,
she thought.
Like the block that moved at her hand.
“It lifts the ship,” said Obsidia. “It carries it, and it hides it. I ride it across the stars.”
“And into this dark?”
“Only through a door wide enough. The body opens one for me, far from any eyes. Or that one.” Her eyes went to the crack.
“Over a city, they’ll see you.”
“They will see that I am there. Not where I came from.”
“And where do you sit, when you command it?”
Obsidia turned her head and looked at her. “What would you do with that?”
“Know it.”
“Where no one finds me, unless I call them.”
Vexana looked back along the ship. Block after block hung from it into the storm. Any one of them could hide the place where she sat.
“And the gate,” said Vexana. “When it’s wide enough, who goes through?”
“One at a time. Whatever is in its mouth must clear it before the other can pass.”
“Which goes first?”
“It is the body’s door. The body.”
“And you?”
“That I decide.”
So the body would come through before anything else, whole, over those lights. Vexana pictured its wings above the bay.
Whole, and close,
she thought.
That is my moment.
She did not ask when. The crack would tell her.
She looked at the dark place at the middle of the star. “And that?”
“A drain,” said Obsidia. “A door held this wide, for this long, grows one at its center. A black hole.”
“It’s growing.”
“With the door. It reaches a short way, no farther. It takes only what has no strength left to hold against it.”
“And the body? Your ship?”
“We keep to the rim. Whatever crosses the middle, it unmakes.”
“And on the other side?”
“Nothing made of matter ever comes back out,” said Obsidia. “I woke at the edge of one.”
Vexana said nothing.
A paper with Chang’e’s name on it.
Status: untested.
One line, where her finger had stopped and stayed. It said an Aspirant’s light would shine on inside a black hole, and come home.
A green-railed roof, and her own voice: “In case.”
She kept her face still. The wind through the crack smelled of rain.
“The Core,” she said. “You said another time.”
The hum sank low under Obsidia’s palm.
“The knot where the Will’s threads to every Ender meet,” said Obsidia. “Break it, and the Will has no hands. Hold it, and the Enders answer whoever holds it.”
Every Ender in those rows,
Vexana thought.
Turning when I said.
“Where is it?”
“I have never seen it. It has never been shown to me.”
“Then where is it?”
“I do not know.”
Weeks of searching the dark. True or a lie, it came to the same: she would not find the Core before the crack was whole.
Then it is the chest, when it opens to fire,
she thought.
Mine alone. Nothing of me after.
Obsidia was watching her face. “Do you still believe you have a choice?”
Vexana’s eyes went to the suit on the slab. To the hand that was still a fist.
Her own hand closed. She did not open it.
“As long as the Aspirant voice echoes, I will resist the darkness,” she said.
Obsidia lifted her palm from the suit. The hum stopped, and the ticking with it.
For a long moment nothing on the prow made a sound.
Aspirant.
The word was out before she could stop it. She had said it in the dark before, alone. Never to anyone.
“Where on earth does that arrogance come from?” said Obsidia.
She did nothing more. Her palm went back over the suit’s core.
Vexana did not move. She had just told the Will’s commander which side she was on.
No Ender up here,
she thought.
Only her. And she let it pass again.
She leaned down toward the crack, to the post the Will had given her.
Behind her the violet hum rose under Obsidia’s palm. In the dead suit’s chest the core ticked once more, and went still.
